part_title: Image Generation, Visual Understanding and Diffusion
review_basis: Original Module 04 numbered WebP slides 8–11 individually inspected: actual labels, diagrams and example probabilities narrated in visual sequence.

scenes.title: Text-to-image generation
scenes.narration: This slide shows how an image-capable generative model turns written instructions into a new picture. Begin with the left prompt: a blue sky with white clouds and the word HELLO spelled in those clouds. The prompt enters the image-capable model in the center, and the arrow leads to a generated picture. No source image was supplied: this is text-to-image, not editing an existing photo. On the right, the human review panel reminds us to inspect the spelling and visual composition, meaning where the objects and shapes are placed. Even when the picture looks attractive, lettering inside generated images can be distorted. The three numbered points below reinforce that the prompt describes the desired scene, text rendering may be imperfect, and a starting image is not needed. A student making a poster might use this to brainstorm an illustration, then check the wording before publication. Question: if you only provide a text description and request a fresh illustration, is this image-to-image generation? No, this is text-to-image generation.

scenes.title: Image-to-image generation
scenes.narration: On the left, we have an existing photograph of a town street, with shops, cars and a distant clock tower. In the center, the text instruction says to render this street in watercolor style. The model uses both the image and that instruction to create the watercolor-like version on the right. The right picture keeps the main street arrangement but changes colors and painting texture. Read the numbered steps below. First, supply a source image that guides composition and layout. Second, describe what to change. Third, inspect the generated output to see whether the important scene details remain correct. Unlike text-to-image generation, the task has an input picture. Still, image-to-image transformation is not an exact pixel-preserving operation; it can change signs, small objects or other details. This can be useful for design exploration, but it needs care when accuracy matters, such as documentary or product photography. Quick check: if we need a legally exact copy of an original sign, can we trust a stylized AI result without checking? No. Verify critical details against the source.

scenes.title: Image-to-text generation
scenes.narration: Now the direction changes. On the upper left is a photo containing one red apple and one orange on a table. The arrow enters a multimodal vision-language model. Multimodal means the system can process more than one form of information, here visual input and text output. The model responds on the upper right with the description One apple and one orange. This is image-to-text: the model analyzes an image and generates words describing it. The lower left panel shows the opposite direction: a written phrase about an apple and an orange is used to generate an image. These two flows must not be confused on the exam. The numbered notes say that a vision-language model can describe an image, but it might misidentify an object or count objects incorrectly. For example, in a stockroom a model could draft a shelf description, but the inventory count should be checked using reliable records or human review. Decision check: is describing the objects in an existing photograph the same task as creating a new photograph from a sentence? No, the input and output modalities are reversed.

scenes.title: Diffusion image generation
scenes.narration: This diagram introduces diffusion models through a cat image. Follow the top training row from left to right. It begins with a clean picture of a cat and shows increasing random visual noise, step by step, until the rightmost example is nearly pure noise. During training, the model learns how to estimate and remove that noise under different conditions. Now move to the bottom generation row, which runs in the reverse direction. The process begins from random noise and repeatedly reduces it, guided by the text prompt on the right: A cat sitting at a computer in a cozy room. The emerging image gradually becomes recognizable and ends with a cat beside a laptop. The generated picture is new; it is not simply restoring the original training picture from the upper row. The lesson is why image generation may require multiple iterative denoising steps rather than immediately drawing a complete result. Image results still require review for details, composition and responsible use. Check: does the model need to retrieve and reproduce the exact cat photo shown in training to generate a new cat picture? No. It uses learned visual patterns to synthesize a new output.
